content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to use categorial grammar induction for the evaluation of the compositionality of emergent languages. 
The authors propose two metrics: CGF (semantic $F_1$ score of the induced grammar) and CGL (relative lexicon size w.r.t. training data), which are shown by experiments to be well correlated with existing metrics for evaluating compositionality.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
- To the best of my knowledge, this is the first work to consider hierarchical semantics in the evaluation of emergent languages.

- The paper is generally clear and easy to follow. 

## Weaknesses 
- I am not convinced by the experiments that we need such a complicated metric for the investigated toy scenario (Section 5.1): for such a setting, simply mapping the tokens to a predefined lexicon and search for all possible combinations would work as well. I expect a more complicated signaling game setup to better show the advantage of the proposed metric. For example, here are several ideas to improve:
  - Including more lexicon entries that are orthogonal to existing ones, e.g., a set of colors that can describe an object together with a shape, following Kottur et al. (2017). 
  - Including more conjunction relations, e.g., "or".
  - Including verbs.

  In addition, I would also expect the correlation between the proposed metric and more challenging types of compositionality. For example, the test set (1) contains some words that are never seen in the training/validation set, or (2) contains sentences in a different distribution of lengths than the training/validation set.

  On the other hand, I would suggest the authors to consider a set of experiments on some rule-based synthetic languages, instead of only experimenting with emergent languages: in these cases, we would have better understanding and control of the quality.

- The authors fail to recognize some recent work in a broader sense, for example,
  - [1] proposes to induce a CCG from grounding signals, and show that such approach has significantly improved the compositionality on investigated tasks. 
  - [2] presents some interesting findings on the compositionality of emergent languages.

  I suggest the authors to do a more careful review on papers they cited and those cited them for a more comprehensive related work discussion.

[1] Mao et al., 2021. [Grammar-Based Grounded Lexicon Learning](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/file/4158f6d19559955bae372bb00f6204e4-Paper.pdf). In NeurIPS. \
[2] Yao et al., 2022. [Linking Emergent and Natural Languages via Corpus Transfer](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=49A1Y6tRhaq). In ICLR.

- The clarity of the paper can be improved. Please see my detailed comments below.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity and Quality**: While the paper is fairly clear to me except a few details, I believe it could be improved. For example, readers may wonder:
- What does #correctly parsed mean in footnote 4? I suppose it's number of correctly (semantically) parsed sentences, if I understood correctly per the ZC'05 paper.
- In your experiments, did you make sure that your agents converged so that the emergent languages are feasible for the evaluation? How did you do this?
- In addition to describe experimental results, it would be good to explain more about your intuition of each correlation, hypothesis on the reasons and further experiments testing your hypothesis. \
I personally found the positive correlation between CGL and loss (Figure 5) a bit counter-intuitive: have you made sure that the validation loss is low enough in all tested models? I would be also a bit skeptical if not: while the validation loss is a fairly reliable indicator of the training status of a model, starting from some random seeds, neural networks sometimes fail to converge -- including models that fail to converge in the analysis sounds very awkward to me.

Clarifying these details will help general ICLR audience to better understand the paper.

**Novelty**: While most techniques in this paper has been proposed for a while, I still think it is a novel approach to apply CG induction on the evaluation of emergent languages.

**Reproducibility**: I think the authors have included sufficient information for the reproduction of the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper presents to use categorial grammar induction as an evaluation metric of the compositionality of emergent languages. While the paper is generally clear and easy to follow, I believe it could be improved in terms of clarity and quality. In addition, I am not convinced by the experiments that we need such a complicated metric for the investigated toy scenario: for such a setting, simply mapping the tokens to a predefined lexicon and search for all possible combinations would work as well. I expect a more complicated signaling game setup to better show the advantage of the proposed metric.

Therefore, I now recommend the paper to be rejected; however, I believe that the investigated problem is valuable and would strongly encourage the authors to improve the paper for a future submission.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a new metric for compositionality based on categorial grammar induction (CGI).
In short, the proposed metric says that when the grammar/parser learned through CGI better represents the data (i.e., it is an accurate parser and a succinct grammar), the language it was trained on is more compositional.
This measure of compositionality improves upon previous measures in a few ways:
  it accounts for hierarchical compositionality beyond mere concatenation as in toposim;
  it is provides a bidirectional mapping from input to meaning, unlike TRE;
  and it takes into account semantics in addition to syntax unlike UGI (van der Wal et al., 2020).
Some experiment are run with a hierarchical-input signalling game to empirically verify the intuitions of this metric.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- [major] The proposed metric improves upon previous metrics in significant ways.
- [minor] The proposed metric yields a parser and grammar which would enable further investigation of the emergent language.
- [minor] The experiments provide moderate evidence for the empirical effectiveness of the metric.
### Weaknesses
- [major] The empirical evaluations are reasonable but neither motivated by broader concerns in the field nor by comparison to compositionality in human language.
- [minor] The proposed metric would have limited applicability due to the requirement of semantically parsing the input space.
- [minor] Compositionality metrics is an over-studied area of emergent language compared to what the metrics could actually be applied to.
- [minor] The environment is artificial in how it incorporates hierarchy.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
- I had an easy time following the structure of the paper, for the most part.
  - My main criticism here is that at the end of the introduction, I had a good idea of what the CGI-based metric was but not how it was going to be tested.
    It would be good to give a roadmap of the paper including what type of evaluation will be done so the reader has a complete mental picture going into the rest of the paper.
- I always recommend using the $\LaTeX$ defaults for figure positioning.
  Figures 4 and 5 have somewhat distracting placement since they break the flow of text.
- In Figure 8, it would be best to repeat the blue bars in each group where they apply.
  I thought at first that the blue/Input bar was 0 for most of the groups, but I think it is implicitly repeated.
### Quality
- The CGF metric is well-formulated, and effectively ties in prior work in NLP to present a useful tool for emergent language research.
  - A weakness, which is mentioned in the paper, is that this metric relies on a semantic parsing of the input space.
    This could be major or minor, but generally speaking, this is a high-detail metric which would naturally require commensurately high-detail data.
  - CGL seems a little underspecified: what exactly is it assuming about compositional and non-compositional languages that make actually correlate with compositionality.
    Maybe explicating this would shed light on why it generally fell short of CGF.
- The experiments are designed to verify basic intuitions of the proposed metric in a controlled setting.
  Additionally, the results provide a moderate corroboration for the intuitions.
- There are two main experimental directions that are lacking in this paper.
  - There is no comparison to well-motivated examples of where other compositionality metrics lack.
    Yes, there is certainly a theoretical/intuitional justification for the proposed metric, but there is no actual, pre-existing problem that is demonstrably solved by the improvements introduced in this metric.
    Does such a problem exist? -- I am not quite sure, but this question is _not_ beyond the scope of the motivation of this paper.
  - There is no comparison to how we expect compositionality to look in human language.
    This point is strongly related to the above one since presumably aligning notions of compositionality in emergent language with those in human language is a key factor in determing most important problems with compositionality meausres.
    While a full comparison along these lines is certainly beyond the scope of this paper, I think even a brief comparison to human language would merit replacing one of the existing experiments.
- Although the presented signalling game does contain hierarchy, it does so in a very artificial way, and it is not clear to what degree it would resemble are more natural environment.
### Novelty
- The proposed metric differs from existing metrics in relevant ways.
  - Toposim: Proposed metric takes into account hierarchy and internal structure of the message and input.
  - TRE: Proposed metric creates a bidirectional mapping which prevents certain degenerate languages from being considered compositional.
  - UGI: Proposed metric takes into account semantics and not just syntax.
- Compositionality metrics have an outsized number of paper written about them.
  This does not mean that it is a solved problem (far from it), but it does mean that the potential impact of this paper limited by the fact that _useful applications_ of compositionality metrics are less often presented compared to the metrics themselves.
### Reproducibility
- The description of the experiment cover all of the major details.
- Since the source was not (yet) released, I cannot evaluate how easy it would be to run the code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I recommend marginal acceptance because while the paper does not present definitive experiments in support of the proposed metric, the metric itself does different in relevant/significant ways from prior work and has potential to be used down the road.
There are concerns about the introduction of yet another metric of compositionality, limited applicability, and the environment used in the evaluation, but this does not undermine the intuitive appeal of the proposed metric.


### Misc.
- "generalization ability" -> "generalizability"
- For experimental analysis, it would be better to use a rank correlation coefficient (e.g., Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho) instead of a linear correlation coefficient (e.g., Pearson's r/rho) since we do not have any a priori reason to think that the metrics would correlate _linearly_ (or if there is, explicitly state that).
- Although not critical, it would be good to cite a work or two that addresses in what way RNNs can/cannot handle hierarchy since the logical structure of the input is being flattened out before feeding it into the model.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
## Summary:
This paper proposes to use CGI (Categorial Grammar Induction) to measure the non-trivial compositionality (i.e., not the simple color+shape case) of the emergent language, which is quite novel and promising. Introducing the classical CGI to emergent language can not only provide a more powerful metric but can also inspire the community to extend the current emergent communication system to more complex languages (e.g., with hierarchical syntax). However, I have several concerns about the current version.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: As discussed in the summary part.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Novel, but a little hard to understand.
content.summary_of_the_review:
## Major -- Why the CGx is better:
IIUC, one of the core contributions of the paper is providing two metrics: CGF and CGL. Then a thorough comparison between CGX and existing metrics, like TRE and topsim, would make the paper stronger. The authors generally compare them in section 4.3 and section 6, but I think the results and explanations are not persuasive enough.
1. How the points in Figure 5,6,7 are generated. Are they generated by sampling at different training time DURING one run, or by experiments under different settings of several runs, AFTER convergence? If it is the first case, then the figures might be a bit misleading, as the high-loss+low CGF points are all underfitting. We can just draw a scatter plot with the x-axis representing time and the y-axis representing test loss and get a high correlation easily, but we cannot treat the training time as a good metric for test loss.

2. To show the effectiveness of CGX, the paper first observe the correlation between CGX and test performance in Fig5 and then show they correlate well with topsim and TRE in Fig6 and 7. I guess those experiments can only prove CGX is comparable with topsim or TRE, not better. To show their superiority, I have the following two suggestions:

- Important: Clearly show the cased where CGX works while topsim and TRE fail (in terms of the compositional generalization ability, i.e., test accuracy);

- Less important: Show CGX is better in other perspectives, like easier to compute, etc., as topsim is hard to calculate when the input space is large.

## Major -- Great idea but hard to understand:
Although I like this paper very much, I struggle to draw a clear big picture of what kind of information CGX is measuring. 

1. Provide concrete examples (even in the appendix). As the paper is in a toy setting, it might not be too hard to give specific examples to show the core concepts, e.g., what is (or is not) a compositional language, and how one language can (or cannot) systematically generalize to test samples. I guess an explanation like AppendixB in [1], Fig6 in [2], or FigA4 in [3] can be really helpful.

2. The game setup in section5.1 has little practical meaning. What is the meaning of AND(AND(Circle, Star))? (I know the author of [2] also uses this example, which is hard to draw a big picture.) I guess using examples like "John and Josh like Mary-->LIKE[AND[J, J], M]" will make the experiments easier to understand.

3. Some of the experimental results are also hard to understand. Like in Figure-4a, the 7232 example. Why do two "2"s represent different things (S\N and N)? After reading Fig9, I guess the number "2" might represent any SQUARE-related operations, but it would be better to directly explain them in the paper.


## Minors and suggestions:
1. IIUC, CGF measures how 'correct' the language is while CGL measures how 'compressed' the language is. These two concepts are quite similar to the expressivity and compressivity mentioned in [4]. Providing more discussions about that might be quite helpful.

2. For Figures 5,6,7. Better to draw a regression line, like Figure5 in [2].

3. The four different languages mentioned in section5.3-3 are really cool. But still, some concrete examples of what these languages be like would help a lot.

In summary, I like but feel a little struggle reading this paper. So my current score is borderline rejection. However, I am happy to raise my score if the major concerns are addressed during rebuttal.

[1] Ren, Yi, et al. "Compositional languages emerge in a neural iterated learning model." ICLR. 2020.

[2] Andreas, Jacob. "Measuring Compositionality in Representation Learning." ICLR. 2018.

[3] Zhou, Hattie, et al. "Fortuitous Forgetting in Connectionist Networks." ICLR. 2021.

[4] Kirby, Simon, et al. "Compression and communication in the cultural evolution of linguistic structure." Cognition 141 (2015): 87-102.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: General Response to Reviewers and Withdrawal Statement
content.comment:
Thank you very much for reviewing our paper.
All reviewers seem to appreciate our idea itself, which is very encouraging.
However, we decided to withdraw it, because we recognize that it still leaves much to be improved.

Summary of Weaknesses:
- We should come up with a more natural situation where emergent language should be hierarchical.
- We should create more complex compositional semantics as an input space.
- We have to clarify the superiority of CGF and CGL to the existing measures TopSim and TRE.
- We have to conduct a broader survey of related work and discuss them.
